title: Exploring Character
description: Last week our discussion about freedom and structure led us into thoughts on character in times of adversity. This week we pick up that thread to see where it takes us. Join us on this journey to the shores of ignorance.
fullDescription: Matt and Michael open with Michael talking to himself. Then things get interesting. They dive into one of the biggest questions they have ever tackled. Can society actually function without God?

keyQuotes.text: "To live is a creative act. It's not to recreate something. It is to create something."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "If there is no God, everything must be permissible."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt (quoting Dostoevsky)

keyQuotes.text: "The highest good is actually abortion. The highest good is actually transgenderism. The highest good is to put miserable people out of their misery. That right there is an example of how far down the disillusionment goes when you become unmoored."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "If you substitute anything for God, your world gets smaller. And God is the only thing that if you don't, you can't substitute. The world will not get smaller. It actually gets bigger."
keyQuotes.speaker: Michael

keyQuotes.text: "I don't have to be God. I can let God be God. I don't have to come up with perfect ideas. I can be creative and say, well, my idea doesn't quite live up. How did it not live up? How can I change that? That's like rest."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

resources.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
resources.description: German philosopher famous for declaring "God is dead" and exploring the consequences of nihilism.

resources.title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
resources.description: Russian novelist. Matt references his line from The Brothers Karamazov: "If there is no God, everything is permissible."

resources.title: Jordan Peterson
resources.description: Canadian psychologist and commentator. Referenced for his ideas on the "good mother fails" and the Beauty and the Beast analogy.

resources.title: Gad Saad
resources.description: Evolutionary psychologist. Matt mentions his book Suicidal Empathy. |

resources.title: Eric Weinstein
resources.description: Mathematician and podcaster. Referenced for his "two nuclei problem" and warnings about humanity's need to disperse to other planets.

resources.title: Brett Weinstein
resources.description: Biologist and commentator. Referenced for his concept of "metaphorical truth."

resources.title: John 3:16
resources.description: Biblical verse: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten son."

resources.title: Howard Hughes
resources.description: American business magnate and aviator. Referenced as someone whose world grew smaller despite growing riches.

resources.title: Canada MAID (Medical Assistance in Dying)
resources.description: Canada's assisted suicide program.

fullDescription: Matt and Michael open with a toast to Glenn Hansard, who passed away that morning at 56. Matt reflects on how musicians he's never met have shaped his life in real, relational ways. This sparks a conversation about what it means to have a relationship with someone you've never met.

title: Seek and you shall find
description: Seek and you shall find. Ask and you shall receive. You might hear these phrases and dismiss them as a petition to the supernatural, but the ideas seem to be woven into the fabric of our consciousness, science, and even…
fullDescription: Matt and Michael open with the paradox of getting your ass kicked and somehow feeling more alive because of it. Matt shares his realization that there is no "there" to arrive at. The car ride IS the destination. Flat tires, closed restaurants, broken grinders. That's not the interruption of life. That IS life.

keyQuotes.text: "I kept asking, are we there yet? And I think I finally realized, like, we are there. This is it. It's the car ride and shit's gonna go wrong and you're gonna get a flat tire and you show up to where you thought you were going and it turns out they're closed on Monday."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "All men are created in the image of God, even the men that don't believe in God. And because all men are created in the image of God, men have morality. Because God has morality, we are created in that image."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt (quoting John Lennox)

keyQuotes.text: "If you optimize for pleasure, you end up in misery. Optimize for the purpose of a thing, you destroy the thing itself."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "The more you love something, the more you reject almost everything in that category and only accept the best."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "I did try to create a heresy, a little heresy of my own. And when I put my final touches on it, I discovered it was orthodoxy."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt (quoting Chesterton)

title: The Lost Art of Waiting
description: Matt and Michael open with a meditation on waiting—something they used to do constantly without realizing it. Remember standing outside school, wondering if your ride forgot you? Or running out of gas on the interstate…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael open with a meditation on waiting—something they used to do constantly without realizing it. Remember standing outside school, wondering if your ride forgot you? Or running out of gas on the interstate with no cell phone? Those moments weren't just inconveniences; they were built-in spaces for our minds to wander, to sit with the unknown, to discover what we weren't looking for.

The conversation spirals through the tension between "builder mode" and presence, the Dunning-Kruger effect of parenting, and why the most honest Oscar speech is simply "I want to thank God." They land on a paradox: the more skilled you become at anything, the less certain you feel.

Along the way: Salvador Dalí's spoon trick, the MMA fighter's fiancée, why Chesterton says true believers in themselves end up in asylums, and whether we're wired for God—or just wired to need something bigger than ourselves.

Cheers y'all 🍻

fullDescription:
Matt and Michael watched Artemis 2 launch into obscurity, then went deeper. They explore the mathematical impossibility of DNA arising by chance: 10^77 odds versus 10^56 atoms in the Milky Way. They discuss self-organized criticality and why systems collapse suddenly. They examine Asimov's Seldon Crisis: the inevitable binary choice point. They contrast Lucifer's "knowledge for myself" with Socratic and Christ-like humility. They unpack nihilism versus meaning through Lord of the Rings archetypes. They examine why David's census brought divine punishment. The seed must die to become a plant. The question is not whether you will die. It is whether you will die for something that matters.

Cheers y'all 🍻

title: Correcting Toward Love
description: Matt and Michael dive deep into the uncomfortable reality that suffering is not just inevitable, but essential for growth. They explore the tension between wanting to avoid pain and the necessity of embracing it to…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael dive deep into the uncomfortable reality that suffering is not just inevitable, but essential for growth. They explore the tension between wanting to avoid pain and the necessity of embracing it to truly live. From Carl Jung's observation that neuroses are alternatives to legitimate suffering, to the humbling realization that wisdom cannot be earned without cost, the conversation winds through marriage, parenting, business, and faith.

They grapple with what it means to "correct toward" something, to have a destination even when you know you'll get lost along the way. Matt shares a personal story about apologizing to his teenage daughters for holding onto outdated rules. Michael reflects on 20 years of business mistakes that finally feel like wisdom. Together they ask: Can we trust people who aren't perfect? Can we be good if we're also bad?

The episode culminates in a raw reflection on Easter and the resurrection. Not the sanitized version, but the brutal reality of what it means for God to enter human suffering completely. Christ is risen. Everything changes.

Cheers y'all 🍻

fullDescription:
# Ep 276: Imitation, Identity & The Courage to Be Yourself

## Title Options

1. **Ep 276: Imitation, Identity & The Courage to Be Yourself**
2. **Ep 276: Do It Again — On Repetition, Fire & Finding Your Voice**
3. **Ep 276: The Shirt That Doesn't Fit — Becoming Who You Are**
4. **Ep 276: Theme & Variation — Imitation as the Path to Authenticity**
5. **Ep 276: What Does Matt Sound Like?**

---

## Description (SoundCloud/Spotify)

Matt and Michael open on the shores — Mission Beach, specifically — and wander through the vastness of the ocean as metaphor for life's uncontrollable forces. They explore self-organized criticality: the single grain of sand that collapses the whole system, and why we resist the small fires that prevent total destruction.

The conversation turns to authenticity. Can you try to be unique without becoming a trope? Matt shares the story of his college roommate asking, "But how does Matt McCloskey sing it?" — a question that still echoes 25 years later. They discuss theme and variation, the Karate Kid, and why creativity requires structure.

They land on family as placeholder — the people who hold your essential self while allowing you to evolve. And finally: God doesn't fall in love with his people. He just is.

Cheers y'all 🍻

title: Sex Dolls, Vinyl Records, and AI — The Search for What's Real
description: Matt and Michael explore the tension between artificial and authentic in the age of AI. Opening with mortality and fatherhood, they spiral through technology's disconnecting effects, the nature of reality, and what it…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael start with death. A healthy forty-six-year-old drops dead, and the conversation turns to what matters when time is short and kids still need raising. Then things get interesting. They dive deep into AI and authenticity, asking what is real and what is most real. Matt predicts a backlash against smartphones and synthetic content, while Michael pushes back with excitement about AI's potential, and they land somewhere in the tension between them. Billy Corgan refuses to touch AI and calls it demonic. Dante puts flattery in the lowest level of hell. Matt connects the dots and argues that if everything becomes fake, we lose the incentive to engage at all. They explore education, relationships, and the sexualization of culture, noting that we live in a highly sexualized society with less sex than ever, where the icon replaces the idol and the idol hollows itself out. Along the way they touch on vinyl records, breast milk, Good Will Hunting, The Matrix, Tom Petty live, and Leonard Cohen versus Jeff Buckley, all circling the same questions. What is a song? What is intimacy? What is truth?

Cheers y'all 🍻

fullDescription:
Matt and Michael return from two very different deserts. Vegas and Big Bend. One all lights and noise, the other all silence and heat.

Ep 278: Two Deserts

Then things get interesting.

Matt shares what it meant to scatter his father's ashes in West Texas. Michael talks about the solitude of crowds. And somewhere around the forty minute mark, the conversation turns into something else entirely. What is AI actually for? What gets lost when we outsource struggle? Why do we need to be broken to become whole? And what happens to a culture that forgets the purpose of things?

They land on teleology, the study of purpose itself. A knife only makes sense if you know it's meant to cut. So what are we meant for? And what happens when we stop asking?

Cheers y'all 🍻

futureThreads.title: The Full C.S. Lewis Poem
futureThreads.body: Matt only partially remembered "Love's As Warm As Tears" and wants to look it up. Could be a full reading and discussion of the poem's paradox.

futureThreads.title: Matt's Essay from Big Bend
futureThreads.body: Matt wrote in his journal about an idea he wants to turn into an essay. He noted: "This is going to be very difficult to write." He could report back on whether he wrote it and what he learned.

futureThreads.title: The Memory of Being Born
futureThreads.body: Matt's strange pre-conscious memory — a crescendo of noise and light resolving into silence. He wrote a Substack piece on it years ago. Could revisit and expand.

futureThreads.title: Eric Weinstein on Trigonometry
futureThreads.body: Matt referenced a recent episode where Weinstein discussed information access vs. leverage, using black powder as an example. Michael hasn't listened yet. Could both listen and discuss.

futureThreads.title: Jonathan Haidt and Teen Phone Use
futureThreads.body: Matt mentioned Haidt's argument that teenagers literally should not have smartphones. Worth a deeper dive into *The Anxious Generation* and whether they agree with the prescriptions.

futureThreads.title: The Medici Family
futureThreads.body: Michael named his roasting company after the Medici family. He referenced their dual legacy — great patronage and horrible corruption. Could explore: what does it mean to name your business after something morally complicated?

futureThreads.title: "For All Mankind" and the Alternate Space Timeline
futureThreads.body: Michael is watching this Apple TV series. Matt hasn't seen it. Could do a watch-together discussion on what NASA might have become without the Challenger stall.

futureThreads.title: Billy Corgan Interview
futureThreads.body: Matt listened to a long interview with Billy Corgan about AI and creativity. Michael hasn't heard it. Could both listen and debate Corgan's anti-AI stance vs. Michael's tool-based view.

futureThreads.title: The Challenger Conspiracy
futureThreads.body: Matt went down a rabbit hole. They laughed about it but didn't fully explore. Could do a lighthearted "conspiracy corner" segment.

futureThreads.title: The Formula for Black Powder
futureThreads.body: Eric Weinstein's example of information we all have access to but never leverage. Matt already forgot it. Could test: what information do we have access to that we never use?

title: Who Unhooked the Earth From the Sun?
description: Michael plays devil's advocate and argues that human societies naturally refine their values over time. Monogamy works better. Less crime is good. These truths emerge through trial and error. Matt pushes back hard.…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael open with Michael talking to himself. Then things get interesting. They dive into one of the biggest questions they have ever tackled. Can society actually function without God?

Michael plays devil's advocate and argues that human societies naturally refine their values over time. Monogamy works better. Less crime is good. These truths emerge through trial and error. Matt pushes back hard. Without truth and love as a fixed reference point, he argues, the word "better" loses all meaning. What looks like natural progress is actually borrowed capital from a civilization built on Judeo-Christian values. They explore Canada's assisted suicide program, the sterilization of young people through the transgender movement, and Nietzsche's warning that removing God does not just remove religion. It unmoors everything.

This one goes deep. It is about what happens when a culture forgets where its values came from. And why substituting anything for God makes your world smaller.

Cheers y'all 🍻

keyQuotes.text: "To live is a creative act. It's not to recreate something. It is to create something."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "If there is no God, everything must be permissible."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt (quoting Dostoevsky)

keyQuotes.text: "The highest good is actually abortion. The highest good is actually transgenderism. The highest good is to put miserable people out of their misery. That right there is an example of how far down the disillusionment goes when you become unmoored."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "If you substitute anything for God, your world gets smaller. And God is the only thing that if you don't, you can't substitute. The world will not get smaller. It actually gets bigger."
keyQuotes.speaker: Michael

keyQuotes.text: "I don't have to be God. I can let God be God. I don't have to come up with perfect ideas. I can be creative and say, well, my idea doesn't quite live up. How did it not live up? How can I change that? That's like rest."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

resources.title: Friedrich Nietzsche
resources.description: German philosopher famous for declaring "God is dead" and exploring the consequences of nihilism.

resources.title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
resources.description: Russian novelist. Matt references his line from The Brothers Karamazov: "If there is no God, everything is permissible."

resources.title: Jordan Peterson
resources.description: Canadian psychologist and commentator. Referenced for his ideas on the "good mother fails" and the Beauty and the Beast analogy.

resources.title: Gad Saad
resources.description: Evolutionary psychologist. Matt mentions his book Suicidal Empathy. |

resources.title: Eric Weinstein
resources.description: Mathematician and podcaster. Referenced for his "two nuclei problem" and warnings about humanity's need to disperse to other planets.

resources.title: Brett Weinstein
resources.description: Biologist and commentator. Referenced for his concept of "metaphorical truth."

resources.title: John 3:16
resources.description: Biblical verse: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten son."

resources.title: Howard Hughes
resources.description: American business magnate and aviator. Referenced as someone whose world grew smaller despite growing riches.

resources.description: Canada's assisted suicide program.

title: Turtles All the Way Down 🐢
description: Matt and Michael wrestle with one of the oldest questions in philosophy. Why does accepting objective meaning make life harder, not easier? They start with nihilism and why almost nobody can actually live it out.…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael wrestle with one of the oldest questions in philosophy. Why does accepting objective meaning make life harder, not easier?

They start with nihilism and why almost nobody can actually live it out. Michael plays devil's advocate for the social contract view of morality. Matt pushes back hard. If your worldview is just preferences, what do you do when Thanos shows up?

The conversation spirals through C.S. Lewis, 1984, Sam Harris's wireless dog fence, and why telling the truth is just easier than lying. They land on the cross as the place where God measures himself by himself and absorbs the gap we cannot close.

Cheers y'all 🍻

keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

resources.title: C.S. Lewis, The Abolition of Man
resources.description: Lewis's classic work on objective value and the "tao." Matt read this aloud to his mother while camping in Big Bend. He and his mom have been discussing it and sharing interviews about it since. -

resources.title: C.S. Lewis, Mere Christianity
resources.description: Referenced for Lewis's insight that "only people who have tried very hard to be good understand anything about badness." -

resources.title: George Orwell, 1984
resources.description: Discussed for the concept of "we have always been at war with Eastasia" — the revisionist history mechanism where the Party suddenly switches enemies and claims it was always so. -

resources.title: Carl Trueman, The Rise and Triumph of the Modern Self
resources.description: Referenced in an interview on Socrates in the City. Trueman's thesis: pre-modern people defined themselves by externalities (family, land, vocation), while modern people define themselves by internal choices and preferences. -

resources.title: Sam Harris
resources.description: Referenced as someone who has "installed his own wireless dog collar" — refusing to engage with questions that would challenge his materialist worldview. Matt compares him to a dog with an invisible fence who stops dead at arbitrary boundaries.

resources.title: Jordan Peterson
resources.description: Referenced as someone who invites people to "come play" beyond their boundaries, contrasted with Harris who stays within his fenced plot.

resources.title: Wesley Huff
resources.description: Referenced for his line on Joe Rogan: "Give me one miracle and I'll explain everything to you." Either the Big Bang or the virgin birth — pick your miracle.

resources.title: Albert Camus
resources.description: Referenced for his idea that suicide is the ultimate expression of free will, and that "defiance against meaninglessness" was a viable posture.

resources.title: The Lion King (1994)
resources.description: Matt uses Simba's arc as a metaphor for nihilism: naivety → catastrophe → "Hakuna Matata" (nihilism) → wisdom/return.

resources.title: Socrates in the City
resources.description: YouTube channel featuring interviews with intellectuals. The Carl Trueman interview was watched by Matt and his mom. -

resources.title: Thanos
resources.description: Used as a thought experiment: if someone with arbitrary power decides your social contract is wrong, what do you do? You either accept it or fight, and fighting requires objective justification.

title: Over My Dead Body
description: Matt and Michael dive deep into the meaning of Jesus Christ's death and resurrection. Starting from last week's cliffhanger about whether Jesus had to die, they explore the story of Cain and Abel, the problem of human…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael dive deep into the meaning of Jesus Christ's death and resurrection. Starting from last week's cliffhanger about whether Jesus had to die, they explore the story of Cain and Abel, the problem of human sin, and why God chose to meet humanity in its darkest place rather than simply forgive from a distance. The conversation weaves through Job, the cross as the ultimate expression of love, and why this story demands a response that other worldviews don't.

They discuss Carl Jung's Answer to Job, CS Lewis's analogy of God outside of time, and why Christianity's claim of divine self-sacrifice is unique among world religions. Michael shares his experiential journey through multiple religions and why Jesus was the one that actually changed him. Matt reflects on seeing a Rothko painting at the Met and how biblical stories are interactive in a way art cannot be.

The episode grapples with troubling questions: What kind of God commands slaughter? What does it mean that God justifies himself to Job? Why did God choose to die rather than simply forgive? And what does it mean that we are all Cain?

Cheers y'all 🍻

keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "Identity is not defined internally. It is given. It is given through relationship."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "All men are created equal. Erase the last word — people still agree. Erase 'created' — people are shocked. The sentence is only coherent when you keep the word created because it has to do with intent, not with observable, measurable attributes."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "Experientially, I'm all in. I don't understand it. I've tried every single religion... and Jesus was the thing that actually changed me."

resources.title: Answer to Job
resources.description: by Carl Jung — Jung's psychological analysis of the Book of Job and its connection to the Incarnation. Matt references Jung's observation that God's response to Job is the first time in religious history a deity stoops to justify himself to humanity, foreshadowing Christ.

resources.title: The Bible
resources.description: Referenced throughout: Genesis (Cain and Abel), Exodus (Moses and the golden calf), Job, the Gospels, Paul's letters.

resources.title: Jordan Peterson
resources.description: Referenced for his discussion of biblical narratives as living, continuously happening stories. Also mentioned: his observation that "what do you mean by happen? It is happening all the time."

resources.title: C.S. Lewis
resources.description: Referenced for his analogy of God outside of time like an author outside a story, and the idea that God has spent more time thinking about each person than all the seconds of their life.

resources.title: Jonathan Pageau
resources.description: Referenced for his observation about the story of Peter and Judas as an answer to whether Cain could have been redeemed.

resources.title: Mark Rothko
resources.description: Matt's analogy about seeing a Rothko painting in person at the Met and being transfixed, comparing it to engaging with biblical stories interactively.

resources.title: T.S. Eliot
resources.description: Michael references Eliot's poetry as grasping for words to explain the unexplainable.

resources.title: Dostoevsky
resources.description: Mentioned for having epilepsy and writing his best work before seizures.

resources.title: Gad Saad
resources.description: Referenced for the concept of "suicidal empathy."

resources.title: Michael Jordan / Scottie Pippen
resources.description: Used as analogies for hard work and sacrifice.

resources.title: Stan Lee
resources.description: Michael's analogy for God entering his own story (like Stan Lee's cameos).

resources.title: The Chosen
resources.description: TV series about the life of Jesus. Matt mentions watching it and noticing Jesus's habit of giving people nicknames.

resources.title: The Matrix
resources.description: Michael's analogy about Neo learning "that is not air you're breathing" as a metaphor for waking up to spiritual reality.

resources.title: Oklahoma! (musical)
resources.description: Matt references the song "Trouble with a capital T that rhymes with P that stands for pool."

factChecks.explanation: The Latin "excruciare" means "to torture, torment," from "crucifigere" (to crucify). The word "excruciating" literally means "from the cross."

factChecks.claim: More historical corroboration for Jesus's resurrection than almost any other ancient event
factChecks.explanation: Even skeptical scholars like Bart Ehrman agree Jesus existed and was crucified; the resurrection claim is debated but the historical facts surrounding it (crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, empty tomb traditions, disciples' belief in resurrection appearances) are among the best-attested events in ancient history.

factChecks.claim: Cain's bloodline created first weapons of war and established cities
factChecks.status: Genesis 4:17-22 describes Cain's descendants as founders of cities (Enoch), tent-dwellers, musicians, and metalworkers (including Tubal-Cain, "forger of all instruments of bronze and iron").

factChecks.claim: No other religion has God dying for humanity
factChecks.explanation: Most world religions emphasize human effort (prayer, meditation, good works, ritual) to reach the divine. Christianity's claim of divine self-sacrifice is unique among major world religions.

factChecks.claim: Dostoevsky wrote best before epileptic seizures
factChecks.status: Documented in his letters and biographies
factChecks.explanation: He described pre-seizure "ecstatic" states that he associated with creative insight.

title: Why Do We Call Successful People Dumb?
description: Matt and Michael start with breath work and singing, and wander into why good things become mechanical, why we turn truths into idols, and what it costs to actually participate in the world. Then the strange phenomenon…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael start with breath work and singing. Then things get interesting. They wander into why good things become mechanical. Why we turn truths into idols. And what it costs to actually participate in the world.

The conversation spirals through novelty and monotony. Tools that optimize life but drain the life out of living. The strange phenomenon of calling accomplished people dumb. And the DNC's refusal to learn from defeat.

Cheers y'all 🍻

title: The Madness of a World Without Reason
description: Matt and Michael dive into three recent news stories that have them asking the same question. What is this madness? They break down the California mayoral race, the Karmelo Anthony murder trial, and the Somali World Cup…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael dive into three recent news stories that have them asking the same question. What is this madness? They break down the California mayoral race, the Anthony Carmelo murder trial, and the Somali World Cup referee denied entry to the US. But the headlines are just the entry point. The real conversation is about something deeper. Why does it feel like half the country has stopped operating in good faith? Why do people defend narratives at the cost of reality itself? And what happens to a culture when it unhooks itself from any higher ideal?

Matt brings in John C. Lennox's argument that atheism, taken to its logical conclusion, unwinds rationality completely. If your brain is the product of a purposeless process, why would you trust it to do science or even to claim you are rational? The guys connect this to Nietzsche's warning about unhooking the earth from its sun, and to C.S. Lewis's insight from The Screwtape Letters about directing malice toward neighbors and benevolence toward strangers we will never meet.

They also get personal. Michael talks about being in love with the idea of his wife and kids versus actually loving them. Matt quotes Teresa of Avila. God, I don't love you. I don't even want to love you, but I want to want to love you. The episode lands on a hard truth. Without a shared goal, there is no progress. And right now, we do not even agree that there should be a goal.

Cheers y'all 🍻

futureThreads.body: Michael explicitly bookmarks this at 97:24: "Dude, I feel like there's a whole conversation in that area." Matt agrees: "Well, maybe we should bookmark it." The thread: Jesus telling Peter "look at me" as he sinks into the water connects to the father-child relationship, where "look at me" is life and death when you're young but becomes less legitimate as children grow. They want to explore how this dynamic plays out spiritually, relationally, and culturally.

futureThreads.body: Referenced at 38:47 when Matt talks about watching high school football players who start out pretending and eventually become the real thing. Michael connects this to his own point about living a lie versus aspiring to become something better. This could be a full conversation about identity formation, discipline, and the gap between who we are and who we want to become.

futureThreads.title: The Moral Circle - Conservatives vs. Liberals
futureThreads.body: Matt references a graph at 72:21 showing how liberals rate things as more important the farther they are from themselves, while conservatives rate things as more important the closer they are. Michael responds that if you overlapped the two graphs, you'd have full coverage. They agree this tension is beautiful and necessary, but they only scratched the surface. A full episode on moral circles, proximity vs. distance, and how to hold that tension without it becoming perverted.

futureThreads.title: Words, Definitions, and Communication
futureThreads.body: Matt's extended riff at 85:34 about how we don't use words based on their definitions but on shared understanding, and how bad actors exploit this by swapping definitions without telling anyone. He gives examples: pandemic, vaccine, racism, privilege. This is a rich topic they could return to with more structure.

futureThreads.title: The Kingdom of Heaven
futureThreads.body: Matt mentions at 25:31 that they could talk about the kingdom of Heaven in the context of narrative protection and reality denial. They never fully got there. This remains an open thread from earlier episodes as well. **The Revolutionary War and the 250th anniversary** - Matt expresses frustration that the anniversary is being missed as an opportunity for reconciliation. They could do a full episode on founding principles, what makes America unique, and why the founding story matters now. **Trust in institutions** - Both men agree trust has broken down over the last 6-10 years. They could explore which institutions, why, and whether any are recoverable. **Marriage as a model for cultural cooperation** - The extended metaphor at 46:12 about marriage requiring a shared external reference point could be expanded into a conversation about covenant, vows, and what makes relationships and societies work. **Genocide of reality** - Matt's provocative framing at 27:01 about abolishing reality itself being a kind of spiritual genocide. This connects to their ongoing conversations about Cain, the crucifixion, and modern culture wars. **John C. Lennox** - Matt and Michael both express admiration. A conversation with Lennox about rationality, science, and faith would fit their ongoing thread perfectly. **Someone from Hillsdale College** - Given how much Matt praises their founding history videos, a historian or professor from Hillsdale could add depth to their American history discussions. **Matt Walsh** - They reference his documentary *Am I a Racist?* and the confrontation with Robin DiAngelo. Walsh's approach to cultural commentary aligns with their concerns about narrative over reality.

title: The Proper Posture When Nothing's Working
description: Matt and Michael explore what it means to have the right posture when life isn't going your way. They start with the universal temptation to blame others or wallow in self-pity, then spiral into deeper territory: the…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael explore what it means to have the right posture when life isn't going your way. They start with the universal temptation to blame others or wallow in self-pity, then spiral into deeper territory: the scapegoat impulse, the maturing conscience, and what it actually means to "seek first the kingdom of heaven." Matt shares raw reflections on a year and a half of job searching, moments where he shied away from hard conversations, and what he learned by writing out 25 years of career history. Michael brings in Brother Lawrence, the toddler's astonishment at everything, and the difference between turning an icon into an idol. The conversation lands on a powerful truth: the kingdom of heaven isn't a deferred reward. It's here and now, found in recognizing the person in front of you, doing the dishes with gratitude, and loving without expecting anything back. Matt closes with a vulnerable story about raising his kids through a contentious divorce and the unexpected gift he never knew to ask for.

resources.title: Brother Lawrence
resources.description: (17th-century Carmelite monk) — Known for finding God in mundane daily tasks like washing dishes and sweeping floors. Author of The Practice of the Presence of God. - Wikipedia: - Book:

resources.title: René Girard
resources.description: French historian and literary critic whose work on mimetic desire and the scapegoat mechanism influenced Michael's framing of blame as a natural human impulse. - Wikipedia:

resources.title: Fyodor Dostoevsky
resources.description: Referenced by Matt for the argument that "if there is no God, man should be permitted anything" (from The Brothers Karamazov).

resources.title: The Scapegoat Mechanism
resources.description: Michael references the Jewish/Christian scapegoat tradition (Leviticus 16) where sins are symbolically placed on a goat and sent into the wilderness. He connects this to the human impulse to project blame onto others rather than confront our own role in problems.

resources.title: Rdio
resources.description: Early music streaming service (2010–2015) that Michael references as a cautionary tale. Known for exceptional design and UX but failed because they never invested in marketing or sales. Postmortem analysis cited by Matt. - Wikipedia:

resources.title: Field of Dreams
resources.description: 1989 film with the famous line "If you build it, he will come." Matt and Michael use this as a metaphor for the builder's fallacy: creating something beautiful but failing to tell anyone about it. - IMDb:

resources.title: "Mom, why are we poor? Because your dad got Claude Code and never shipped anything"
resources.description: Meme referenced by Matt about AI coding tools enabling endless tinkering without shipping products.

resources.title: Jordan Peterson
resources.description: Referenced by Matt for his argument that "the more you think about yourself, the more miserable you become" and the therapeutic value of directing attention outward.

resources.title: The All In Podcast
resources.description: Matt mentions hearing similar arguments about self-focus and misery on this podcast.

resources.title: Cain and Abel
resources.description: Biblical story referenced by Matt (Genesis 4). Cain's sacrifice is rejected; God tells him "if you do what is right, will you not be accepted?" Matt uses this as a framework for the proper posture: making better sacrifices (spending time better) rather than resenting outcomes.

resources.title: Pinocchio / Jiminy Cricket
resources.description: Matt uses the story of Pinocchio developing his conscience through life experience as a metaphor for the maturing conscience. Jiminy Cricket starts as a "shitty conscience" but develops over time.

title: Are You Feeling Semiquincentennial?
description: Matt and Michael dive into America's 250th birthday and ask why we're so reluctant to celebrate it. They explore how patriotism became politically coded, the strange guilt of prosperity, and why the founders' vision of…
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael dive into America's 250th birthday (the semiquincentennial) and ask why we're so reluctant to celebrate it. They explore how patriotism became politically coded, the strange guilt of prosperity, and why the founders' vision of property rights and freedom of speech created unprecedented human flourishing.

The conversation spirals through the Dunning-Kruger effect, democracy as truth-discovery, and the Orwellian rewriting of history. They touch on the intolerance of tolerance, what it means to hold two truths at once, and Michael's grandfather's immigrant story of escaping the mines through sheer will.

The episode lands on a hard truth. If you stop celebrating what's good, you shouldn't be surprised when you get less of it.

Cheers y'all 🍻

resources.description: by George Orwell — Dystopian novel about totalitarianism, surveillance, and the rewriting of history. Winston Smith's job was literally to rewrite historical records to match the current party line.

resources.title: The Rise and Triumph of the Modern Self
resources.description: by Carl Trueman — Explores how the modern Western understanding of selfhood emerged and why rewriting history is essential to postmodern movements. Matt recommends the section on why history gets rewritten.

resources.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death
resources.description: by Neil Postman — Postman's critique of how television (and by extension, social media) reshapes public discourse into entertainment rather than rational argument.

resources.title: Lincoln
resources.description: (2012, dir. Steven Spielberg) — Daniel Day-Lewis portrayal of Lincoln's political maneuvering to pass the 13th Amendment. Matt specifically recommends this for understanding how delicate and complex ending slavery actually was.

resources.title: Real History with Matt Walsh
resources.description: Documentary series by Matt Walsh. Episode mentioned: the one about slavery and indentured servitude, including the claim about George Washington's runaway slave ad on the day the Revolutionary War began.
(TV series) — Paramount+ series about immigrants traveling the Oregon Trail. Referenced as an example of why people endured hellish journeys to come to America.

resources.title: George Washington
resources.description: First U.S. President. Discussion of his slave ownership (inherited through marriage), his plan to release slaves, and the runaway slave ad allegedly placed on the day the Revolutionary War began.

resources.title: Cosimo de' Medici
resources.description: Early Medici patriarch who understood the danger of flaunting wealth and power. His sons Piero and Lorenzo began flaunting it, leading to Medici troubles.

resources.title: Elon Musk
resources.description: Referenced as the most productive/successful person maybe ever, and the target of resentment despite his contributions. SpaceX valuation discussed (~$1 trillion at time of recording, not $14 trillion as initially suggested).

resources.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect
resources.description: Cognitive bias where unskilled people overestimate their ability, while highly skilled people underestimate theirs. Matt gives the proper definition: it's about self-reporting accuracy, not just "stupid people think they're smart."

resources.title: Chesterton's Fence
resources.description: Principle that you shouldn't remove a fence until you understand why it was put there. Applied to social and economic policies.

resources.title: Preference Falsification
resources.description: Concept from Timur Kuran (though not named): people hide their true preferences in public. Referenced via the Ted Lasso anonymous suggestion box scene.

resources.title: Taylor Lorenz
resources.description: Journalist referenced via a meme about shoveling criticism over a wall, then crying oppression when it gets thrown back.

resources.title: Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)
resources.description: Three recently elected congressmen in New York mentioned as openly anti-American. One allegedly said she would use the American flag as a napkin.

resources.title: Eric Adams / NYC Mayoral Race
resources.description: Referenced in discussion about why people voted certain ways and the tendency to reduce complex political decisions to racism.

resources.title: Gavin Newsom / California
resources.description: Referenced regarding businesses leaving California due to regulation and taxes.

resources.title: Mandavi / Rent Control NYC
resources.description: Referenced regarding NYC rent control policies and their disincentivizing effect on property investment.

resources.title: Bernie Sanders & Elizabeth Warren
resources.description: Referenced as politicians who understand economics but play a part for political mobilization. Warren was a Harvard professor.

resources.title: Trump 2016 Election
resources.description: Discussed as an example of preference falsification and the failure of polls/elites to perceive reality.

resources.title: Rome
resources.description: Referenced as lasting 500-600 years but with questionable continuity due to falls and breakups.

resources.title: UK's Role in Ending Slavery
resources.description: British naval efforts to stop the slave trade on the high seas, described as morally motivated.

resources.title: Indentured Servitude
resources.description: Discussion of white Europeans who sold themselves into servitude as passage to America. Claim: on the day the Revolutionary War began, George Washington's runaway slave ad included 3 Black and 8 white individuals.

resources.title: Continental Congress / Declaration of Independence
resources.description: The founders' courage and foresight in crafting a constitution that has lasted 250 years.

resources.title: Ted Lasso
resources.description: Anonymous suggestion box scene referenced as an example of how to discover true preferences ("wanker").

resources.title: John Denver / Bon Jovi
resources.description: Referenced regarding the US Men's National Team soccer game atmosphere ("Country Roads" and "Livin' on a Prayer" played in stadium).

fullDescription:
Ep 286: Pass the Salt (I Love You)

Matt and Michael explore language itself — how the same sentence can carry seven different meanings depending on which word you emphasize. From Christopher Walken's acting advice to watching a toddler learn to speak, they examine how we communicate far more than dictionary definitions. This spirals into the central claim of John's Gospel: Jesus Christ is the Word. What does it mean that the creative power of the universe is linguistic? And why do we so often use language to hide rather than reveal? They move through imposter syndrome, scripted relationships, and the death of authentic communication in a transactional culture. The conversation lands on forgiveness and repentance as the antidote to false representation, and asks whether our deepest divide isn't political but spiritual.

Cheers y'all 🍻

title: The Cartesian Crisis
description: Matt and Michael wrestle with a question that has been hanging over both of them. Why have they stopped paying attention to the news? Is that a good thing or a bad thing? They land on the idea of a Cartesian crisis.…
fullDescription: Matt and Michael wrestle with a question that has been hanging over both of them. Why have they stopped paying attention to the news? Is that a good thing or a bad thing? They land on the idea of a Cartesian crisis. Nobody trusts anything anymore. Every headline is met with an actually from someone who thinks they have the real truth. They explore how skepticism can lead to nihilism or to wisdom, and why character assassination has replaced actual argument. Then things get interesting. The conversation turns to what it means to truly love someone versus simply labeling them, why we have lost the definition of racism, and how dress codes and tattoos are really just signals we send to the world about who we want to be. They contrast David Bowie and Bob Dylan as two models of subversion, one grounded and one spinning off into the void. They talk about Jung, individuation, and why growing up means learning to reincorporate what you once rebelled against. And they end with a story about a fake recruiter that captures just how deep the trust crisis really goes. Cheers y'all 🍻

keyQuotes.text: "Skepticism is going to turn to nihilism, and that's a problem if it stops there. And what you should do is push past nihilism into wisdom. But skepticism is sort of the door that leads you to one or two of those things. I think we have to be skeptical about our skepticism a little bit."

My dad used to say to me when my son was younger and he was really angry about our divorce, he used to say, I think that's because you're safe to be angry with. He's angry, and he's showing you your anger because you're safe to do that with. And he's like, I think you should be that for him. And that's that. I mean, all relationship is resistance. It's pressure, it's tension. And Jacob wrestles with God, which is to say, what? Something like, he wrestles with truth. He wrestles with ultimate reality, and ultimate reality wrestles back."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "If you think you have the truth. No, I've got it. You don't. You try to possess it, you die. I mean, just think about a relationship, a romantic relationship in which you try to possess the other person. I mean, what does that even mean, to inhabit them, to own them, for them to be yours in some sort of possessive way? I mean, a possessive girlfriend is generally thought of as. That's not what you want, Right. Maybe what is good dies when you claim to have the ultimate truth, you claim to have morality and others don't, rather than taking the proper position. Or maybe the alternative position, which is we all have access to it, none of us has it because we're all clearly fucked up anyway. We all must submit to it."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "I think what love does is actually looks at us and actually looks at the kind of person we are, not at the kind of agreement that we would like to have, but says, I see some things at odds in you. On the one hand, I've known you to be very kind and generous with me, and on the other hand, I'm seeing you treat this other person in a way that's not commiserate with that. I'm noticing that. Is that what you want to do? Is that who you want to be? Seems to me like you've shown me that you want to be something different. And I think love says, you know, hey, you were manipulative just there. And I don't like to think of myself as a manipulative kind of person. Love says, yeah, but. But you are. That was there. You just did it, and it's okay. I forgive you. You should look at that though, you know, and come to terms with that."

futureThreads.title: The "Judeo-Christian" Debate
futureThreads.body: Matt mentions at [04:57] that Twitter was hot with a battle over the term "Judeo-Christian," with Jordan Peterson weighing in and many names Matt knows coming out against him. Michael says at [78:43] he'll have to look into it and is curious to hear Matt's take. **Suggested follow-up:** Dedicate an opening segment to unpacking this debate and where each of them lands.

futureThreads.title: The Nature of Racism — Deeper Dive
futureThreads.body: They touched on this extensively ([14:32]–[35:32]) but didn't resolve it. Matt explicitly says at [33:55] he wants to put a sharper definition on the term because "we've lost the term. I don't think we really know what racism is anymore." They discussed stereotypes, dress codes, signaling, and the difference between noticing reality and being prejudiced. **Suggested follow-up:** A full episode on race, stereotypes, and what healthy judgment actually looks like.

futureThreads.title: Transgender Identity and the Will to Control Reality
futureThreads.body: Matt briefly touches on this at [41:51] as an extreme form of demanding reality conform to the self rather than submitting to it. He explicitly says "maybe in its extreme forms, trans is a kind of that." This is a thread they didn't fully pull. **Suggested follow-up:** A careful, good-faith conversation about gender identity, bodily autonomy, and the philosophical tension between self-creation and submission to reality.

futureThreads.title: The Collapse of Trust in Institutions / Information Ecosystem
futureThreads.body: Matt's recruiter scam story ([65:38]) and the broader theme of the Cartesian crisis could be its own episode. They ask: "Where is this going to drive us?" and suspect it will drive many people to God. **Suggested follow-up:** How do you rebuild trust once it's broken? What institutions, if any, are still trustworthy?

futureThreads.title: Art, Authenticity, and the Audience
futureThreads.body: The David Bowie vs. Bob Dylan contrast ([49:42]) opened up rich territory about what artists owe their audience, the difference between subversion and nihilism, and why some artists burn out while others endure. Paul McCartney and The Beatles' drug use came up as a related thread. **Suggested follow-up:** What makes art "true"? Is caring about your audience a betrayal of artistic integrity or the whole point?

futureThreads.title: Parenting, Rebellion, and Letting Kids Individuate
futureThreads.body: Matt talks about wanting his kids to rebel to some degree ([60:04]) and the responsibility of elders to provide structure while allowing individuation. Michael connects this to his own daughters and conversations about tattoos and nose rings. **Suggested follow-up:** A parenting-focused episode on raising kids who can think for themselves without spinning off into the void.

futureThreads.title: The Recruiter Scam / AI and Identity
futureThreads.body: Matt's detailed story about the fake recruiter with the stolen LinkedIn profile ([65:38]–[68:47]) is a vivid example of a larger phenomenon. **Suggested follow-up:** How is AI and deepfake technology making it impossible to verify identity? What does that mean for hiring, dating, and basic social trust?

fullDescription:
Matt and Michael open with the Texas heat and the strange feeling of being between seasons. Not just summer tipping toward fall, but the inner seasons of thought and spirit where old ideas fade and new ones haven't arrived. What do you do when you don't know what to do? They explore anxiety and faith, the discipline of presence, and how focusing on relationships unlocked unexpected reconnections.

Then things get deeper. They wrestle with truth as conforming to reality, the fear of God as respect for overwhelming power, and why rights only work when they come from God rather than government. The conversation turns to communism and why it always ends in genocide, why markets and elections work because they let reality speak, and why everything good is good because of love. Michael calls it what it is. Two guys stumbling through ideas, pushing on things, trying to find the meat on the bone.

Cheers y'all 🍻

keyQuotes.text: "The past is forgiven, the present is full of power, and the future is full of hope."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt, [05:36] (quoting Streams in the Desert)

keyQuotes.text: "Truth is conforming oneself to reality. So many of us don't want to conform to reality. We want reality to conform to us. And reality doesn't do that."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "Wisdom is ultimately humility. Wisdom is, I don't know the right answer."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "You can't define it ahead of time. Life is an adventure. It has to be lived that way."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "Anything that's good is good because of love. And someone who loves something wants to talk about it and share about it. It's an act of worship."
keyQuotes.speaker: Matt

keyQuotes.text: "Sometimes you need to go and spend time away from people and with God. And other times you need to be with people and participate in that."
keyQuotes.speaker: Michael

keyQuotes.text: "If you don't have something greater to reference, it really boils down to power."
keyQuotes.speaker: Michael

fullDescription:
Matt and Michael open with a toast to Glenn Hansard, who passed away that morning at 56. Matt reflects on how musicians he's never met have shaped his life in real, relational ways. This sparks a conversation about what it means to have a relationship with someone you've never met.

The conversation deepens into attention. What are you fixing your eyes on? They explore the bronze serpent in the wilderness, Jesus telling Peter to look at him, and how Instagram's algorithm quietly answers that question for most people. Michael shares that his why needs an upgrade after years of survival mode. Matt argues that don't die is not a sufficient reason to live. You need something positive to move toward.

They close with the extraordinary privilege of being alive right now. A handwritten Bible from 1402 was chained to a cathedral shelf. Today you can read it on your phone in seconds. The options for where to fix your eyes are nearly infinite, which makes the question more urgent than ever.

Cheers y'all 🍻

fullDescription:
Matt and Michael mark eight years of the podcast with a question someone recently asked Michael. Does the devil exist? What follows is a winding conversation through evil, morality, materialism, and the logic of the cross. They explore why Western culture has lost touch with the concept of evil, how political contradictions reveal our moral confusion, and why the devil's greatest trick might be making himself disappear from the conversation entirely. Drawing on prison interviews, biblical texts, Solzhenitsyn, Scott Peck, and even Thanos, they land on a surprising conclusion. The devil is real, but he's not who we think he is. He's the spirit of self-justification, the voice that says "I am enough." And we all hear it.

title: We Are There Yet
description: Matt and Michael open with the paradox of getting your ass kicked and somehow feeling more alive because of it...
fullDescription:
Matt and Michael open with the paradox of getting your ass kicked and somehow feeling more alive because of it. Matt shares his realization that there is no "there" to arrive at. The car ride IS the destination. Flat tires, closed restaurants, broken grinders. That's not the interruption of life. That IS life.

Then things get deep. They wrestle with Dawkins vs. Lennox on justice and whether the universe has a moral order. They explore why science itself presupposes God, why atheism requires its own kind of faith, and why Lennox's answer about morality is devastating. All men are created in the image of God, even the ones who don't believe in Him.

The back half dives into inversion. How we try to make reality conform to us instead of conforming ourselves to reality. They tackle sex, polyamory, pornography, and C.S. Lewis's insight from The Abolition of Man. If you optimize for the purpose of a thing, you destroy the thing itself. Optimize for pleasure, and you end up in misery.

Cheers y'all 🍻

keyQuotes.text: I kept asking, are we there yet? And I think I finally realized, like, we are there. This is it. It's the car ride and shit's gonna go wrong and you're gonna get a flat tire and you show up to where you thought you were going and it turns out they're closed on Monday.
keyQuotes.author: Matt

keyQuotes.text: All men are created in the image of God, even the men that don't believe in God. And because all men are created in the image of God, men have morality. Because God has morality, we are created in that image.
keyQuotes.author: Matt (quoting John Lennox)

keyQuotes.text: If you optimize for pleasure, you end up in misery. Optimize for the purpose of a thing, you destroy the thing itself.
keyQuotes.author: Matt

keyQuotes.text: The more you love something, the more you reject almost everything in that category and only accept the best.
keyQuotes.author: Matt

keyQuotes.text: I did try to create a heresy, a little heresy of my own. And when I put my final touches on it, I discovered it was orthodoxy.
keyQuotes.author: Matt (quoting Chesterton)

Career FG% was 49.7%, not 7%. The 7% figure likely refers to "success rate" in a broader sense (championships vs. seasons, iconic moments vs. total games). Needs context.
Commonly cited stat. BLS data shows ~20% fail in year 1, ~50% by year 5. The "1 in 10" is a rough approximation for long-term survival.

factChecks.explanation: Widely attributed to Gretzky. Verified.

factChecks.claim: Margaret Thatcher "The problem with socialism is you eventually run out of other people's money"
factChecks.explanation: Attributed to Thatcher. She said "socialism" not "communism" as Matt quoted. Minor misquote.
Multiple studies confirm married/cohabiting couples report higher sexual frequency than singles. Verified.

factChecks.claim: Children respond to seeing biological parents' love
factChecks.explanation: Research in developmental psychology supports that children show positive emotional responses to parental affection. The specific claim about step-parents not eliciting the same response is more nuanced and varies by study.
